title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Pittsfield tightens zoning while voters reject projects and back opponents across Michigan.

lines.text: Good evening and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Friday night and the big story tonight is Pittsfield Township moving to tighten its zoning rules on data centers after residents spoke up loud and clear.
Exactly, Graham. This feels like part of something bigger happening all over the state right now.
Let's start with Pittsfield. The township is drafting changes aimed at curbing sprawl after folks raised concerns about noise, traffic, and how much power these facilities pull.
Why Pittsfield specifically, and why now? It's right next to Ann Arbor, so the stakes feel pretty local for a lot of people.
Right, and the rules would hit future projects in that area. Township leaders are looking at safeguards so the grid doesn't get strained without new protections in place.
And if those safeguards aren't there, what happens to electric bills for regular ratepayers?
That's the core worry. Large facilities can draw massive loads, and without planning, utilities might pass costs along. We've seen similar concerns in other townships where projects got proposed.
How far back does this fight go in Washtenaw County? It seems like it's been building.

It has. Earlier this week Augusta Township voters overturned a rezoning that would have allowed a data center on farmland. That kept the land agricultural and avoided the noise, power, and water demands.
Water is another big piece, isn't it? Cooling these places takes a lot.
It does. Residents in several spots have flagged that alongside traffic and how it changes the character of rural or suburban areas.
So Pittsfield is trying to get ahead of it with zoning tweaks. Could this become a model for other Washtenaw townships?
That's what local observers are saying. If it works there, nearby communities might copy the approach to keep some control over where and how big these projects can get.
What about the bigger picture for towns deciding on their own land use? Is this local control winning out?
In a lot of places it looks that way lately. Yesterday Washtenaw voters shot down a billion-dollar rezoning in a rural township, blocking heavy power and water use on what would have been farmland.
And over in western Michigan, Holland-area voters rejected a project at the ballot box after months of debate on noise, power, and property values.
Yes, and that defeat came even after site plans had advanced. It shows organized local opposition can stop things late in the process.
Independence Township in Oakland County took a different route this week with a moratorium. How does that fit in?
Supervisors there approved a pause on new proposals while they write rules. It gives the community time to figure out acceptable levels of power, water, and land use.
That sounds like a practical step. Does it set a template for other Oakland County towns?
It could. Folks watching similar proposals are seeing a clear way to slow things down and get community input first.
Now shifting to the political side, we had some primary results yesterday that tie right into this.
We did. A candidate who campaigned against data center growth won a Democratic primary for state House, moving that fight into the legislature for that district.
And in the congressional race, Will Lawrence beat Haley Stevens in the MI-7 Democratic primary after vowing to block large projects. That puts the issue in front of Congress.
Exactly. Voters in Washtenaw and surrounding counties now have a representative who made opposition to data centers central to the campaign.
What does that mean for power demand and tax breaks at the federal level?
It shifts the conversation to Washington on grid costs and water use, especially since these projects can affect rates far beyond the immediate area.
Back to local courts, Monroe Township is trying to toss a $300 million lawsuit from a developer after it banned new facilities.
Yes, the township wants a federal judge to dismiss the case. It centers on whether local governments can block projects that would pull huge amounts of power and water.
Residents 30 miles away in southeast Michigan have a stake in how that turns out, right?
They do. If the ban holds, it reinforces local authority. If it gets overturned, it could open the door for more projects elsewhere.
In Mason, voters narrowed the city council field in a primary dominated by a proposed data center.
Eight candidates remain. The project has split residents over electricity rates and industrial zoning in Ingham County. November winners will decide if it moves forward.
And another primary win for a moratorium backer is pushing the whole debate into Congress too.
That's right. It gives residents facing new projects a stronger voice in Washington on those grid and water issues.
So pulling it together, Graham, what happens next across these communities?
More townships are likely watching Pittsfield and Independence as examples. Some may adopt similar zoning or moratoriums while the court cases and legislative races play out.
And for folks 30 or 60 miles away who aren't directly in these townships, why should they care?
Because power demand doesn't stay local. Strain on the grid can affect rates regionally, and successful local pushback can influence how the state handles future proposals.
On deck for meetings, anything coming up this weekend or early next week?
Nothing major on the public calendar right now. We'll keep tracking any special sessions or township board dates as they get posted.
Sounds good. Listeners can stay on top of it all.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Pittsfield Cracks Down on Data Centers as Voter Pushback Spreads
